title: When the Provision Breaks
premise: Storm chaser Gideon Quintana, deep in debt to a cheerful loan shark named Marisol Vane, takes a salvage contract to recover equipment from a government survey team that vanished in the Sawtooth Range—gear intact, no bodies, no tracks. In the abandoned camp Gideon finds the surveyors' field journal revealing they discovered an illegal water-diversion scheme feeding a powerful ranching consortium, and that the team didn't vanish; they were hunted. Pursued by the consortium's private security and racing the first snows, Gideon must decide whether to sell the journal to pay their debt or carry it out to expose the truth. The story ends with Gideon delivering the evidence to a journalist at terrible personal cost, settling with Vane on their own terms, and walking out of the range as the passes close behind them.
about_author: Gideon Ishikawa is a former backcountry guide who spent six seasons in the northern ranges before turning to fiction full-time. Their writing draws on real search-and-rescue cases and a lifelong fascination with landscapes that keep secrets.

chapters.title: The Optimist's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In a roadside diner, Marisol Vane cheerfully recalculates Gideon's debt after a failed chase season, offering one clean way out: a salvage contract for government gear left in the high country. Emotional beat: humiliation masked as opportunity, and the first hint that nothing about this job is simple.

chapters.title: Contract of Convenience
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Reviewing the contract, Gideon notices the client is a shell company and the insurance valuation on the lost equipment is absurdly inflated. They sign anyway because winter debt has teeth. Emotional beat: uneasy complicity—the reader watches Gideon choose money over instinct.

chapters.title: Two Hands and a Half Tank
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon recruits Dee Okafor, a disgraced former park ranger who knows the Sawtooth better than any map, paying her with a cut instead of cash. Emotional beat: wary partnership; two people with something to prove sizing each other up over a truck bed of rope and radios.

chapters.title: Where the Trail Forgets Itself
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. The approach through the lower canyons, Dee narrating the land like an old friend while noting details that don't fit: a closed road recently graded, fresh tire tracks from vehicles too heavy for recreation. Emotional beat: creeping wrongness beneath beautiful country.

chapters.title: Camp Four, Untouched
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. They reach the survey team's last camp: tents still pitched, food cached, satellite phone dead but unbroken, and no signs of struggle or departure. Emotional beat: dread crystallizing into certainty—people do not leave gear like this voluntarily.

chapters.title: The Field Journal
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Inside a waterproof case, Dee finds the surveyors' journal documenting flow measurements that make no sense until mapped: a river being quietly bled dry upstream by an unlicensed diversion serving the Corliss Ranching Group. Emotional beat: revelation—the vanishing was not accident but silencing.

chapters.title: What the River Owes
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Following the diversion channel upstream, they find the intake structure and fresh boot prints—someone maintains it regularly. A distant engine forces them off the ridgeline. Emotional beat: from investigators to fugitives in a single afternoon.

chapters.title: Debt Collectors Wear Boots Too
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The consortium's security chief, Halloway, reports to Corliss that 'the salvage crew' found more than gear; meanwhile Gideon realizes their contract was bait to locate the journal. Emotional beat: betrayal reframed—the debt was always the trap.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Their satellite messenger is jammed or dead; a near-miss with a patrol helicopter forces them into a burn scar where visibility is brutal. Dee confesses why she lost her ranger badge—she reported Corliss once before and was buried. Emotional beat: shared history of institutions failing them.

chapters.title: The High Route
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. With the low passes watched, Dee proposes a brutal high route across the range crest ahead of a building storm system—a route Gideon's storm-chaser instincts read like a countdown clock. Emotional beat: commitment; turning back is no longer survivable or thinkable.

chapters.title: Weather Is a Witness
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A fast-moving front hits early. Gideon reads the sky with professional love, using the storm's leading edge to erase their tracks and blind the helicopters. Emotional beat: competence as joy—the first chapter where Gideon's craft is an asset, not a liability.

chapters.title: Halloway
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV. The security chief, a former ranger himself, tracks them with reluctant respect and growing doubt about his employers' methods—he signed on to guard property, not bury surveyors. Emotional beat: the antagonist's conscience flickering awake.

chapters.title: Cold Camp
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. A frozen night in a snow cave, hypothermia gnawing at their margins. Dee and Gideon argue about the journal: sell it to Vane and live, or take it to a reporter and probably die broke. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth made explicit between shivers.

chapters.title: The Second Camp
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. They find the surveyors themselves—not murdered but hiding, three frostbitten survivors led by team lead Ana Reyes, who chose disappearance over trusting any agency Corliss hadn't bought. Emotional beat: relief curdling into fury at how deep the rot runs.

chapters.title: Five Is Slower Than Two
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Moving five people through worsening terrain; Reyes insists on carrying every page of data even as it slows them, while one survivor's frostbite turns septic. Emotional beat: the cost of principle measured in hours and toes.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Saddle
chapters.summary: Halloway's POV, then Gideon's. Halloway corners them at a saddle pass—but having read the journal copies, he lets them pass and stages a false report, buying them a day he may pay for with his life. Emotional beat: an enemy choosing a side.

chapters.title: Whiteout
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The full storm arrives; the injured survivor deteriorates; a cornice collapse nearly takes Reyes and the data case. Gideon makes a navigation gamble through zero visibility guided only by wind memory. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into focus—the storm chaser's final exam.

chapters.title: Vane's Offer
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At a prearranged cache, a message from Marisol: she'll clear the entire debt if Gideon hands over the journal—Corliss is her biggest client, and the salvage contract was her play all along. Emotional beat: the true face of the 'dangerous optimists,' and Gideon's quiet refusal.

chapters.title: The Last Descent
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. The final push down the east slope as the passes close, pursued by a last desperate ground team, the injured survivor carried in a makeshift litter. Emotional beat: everything staked, everyone spent, momentum carrying them past exhaustion.

chapters.title: Signal Fire
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Cornered above the tree line with no escape, Gideon does what a storm chaser does best: uses weather, igniting a signal fire visible for miles that draws both a rescue aircraft and news cameras already tipped by Halloway's anonymous leak. Emotional beat: climax—truth weaponized in public view.

chapters.title: Settlement
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Aftermath in a valley town: the story breaks, Corliss's operation freezes under investigation, and Gideon settles with Marisol—not with the journal, but by selling her out to federal investigators as the contract's architect, walking away owing nothing. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, paid in full.

chapters.title: What the Range Keeps
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Weeks later, Dee and Gideon drive back toward the mountains as the first reliable spring thaw begins; Reyes testifies, Halloway awaits trial as a witness, and the river runs full again. Emotional beat: resolution without absolution—the wilderness forgives nothing, but people, sometimes, start over.
